noteRef.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specPoints.text: understand how water is absorbed by root hair cells

primer.text: A plant is thirsty all the time, yet it has no mouth. Its answer sits underground: root hair cells, microscopic extensions that press into soil water and pull it inward by osmosis before handing it up the plant. This note follows the water from those fuzzy tips right through to the leaf's working cells.

lessons.title: Root Hair Cells and the Uptake into the Root
sourceHeadings: Uptake of water into the root
lessons.opening: Root hair cells are single-cell extensions of the root's epidermis, shaped to absorb water osmotically while drawing mineral ions in by active transport, feeding both inward across the root cortex toward the xylem.
keyPoints: Root hairs enlarge the surface area across which uptake happens.
Water enters the cells by osmosis, down a water potential gradient.
Mineral ions enter by active transport, funded by mitochondria.
The hair extensions reach into the film of water between soil particles.
Absorbed water moves inward toward the xylem at the root's core.

low.restatement: Hair-shaped epidermis cells absorb water by osmosis and ions by active transport, then pass them inward.
low.analogy: A kitchen sponge: the more frilly surface it shows to the spill, the faster it drinks.
low.examPointer: Quote both transport words — osmosis for water, active transport for ions — since one mark often hangs on the pairing.

medium.restatement: The large surface area raises the uptake rate, while mitochondria power the pumps that accumulate ions against their gradient.
medium.analogy: A wide door handles more visitors, and the bouncer (active transport) can push some uphill where they would not go alone.
medium.examPointer: If asked why roots are efficient, name surface area AND the energy supply; one without the other loses a mark.

options.text: Single-cell extensions of the root's epidermis
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
They belong to the root epidermis, and each hair is one cell.
Leaf pores are stomata, a different structure entirely.
Seed storage is not where uptake happens.

check.stem: By which process does water enter a root hair cell?

options.text: Osmosis, down a water potential gradient
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Evaporation belongs to the leaf surface, not the root.
That is a white cell feeding mechanism, not plant uptake.
Condensation is a gas-to-liquid change, not cell uptake.

check.stem: How do root hair cells take in mineral ions?

options.text: By active transport, powered by energy from mitochondria
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: By osmosis along with the water
options.explanation: Ions are not water; osmosis moves water only.
Nothing evaporates at the root hair surface.
Uptake often runs against the gradient, so energy is required.

check.stem: Why does a root hair cell contain many mitochondria?

options.text: To release the energy that active transport of ions demands
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Water is not stored in mitochondria.
Roots are dark; photosynthesis cannot run there.

options.text: To make the cell wall thicker
options.explanation: Walls are built from other materials, not mitochondrial work.

check.stem: Which advantage do the hair-like extensions give the root?

options.text: A greatly increased surface area for faster uptake
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: A shorter route to the leaves
options.explanation: The route upward runs through the xylem, unchanged.
These are underground cells; wind is irrelevant.
Storage is a cortex or seed role, not the hair's job.

check.stem: State the two transport processes a root hair cell uses and what each moves.
check.modelAnswer: Osmosis moves water in, and active transport moves mineral ions in.

check.stem: Name the organelle that powers ion uptake in root hair cells.
check.modelAnswer: Mitochondria release the energy used for active transport.

check.stem: Explain why the shape of a root hair cell suits its absorbing role.
check.modelAnswer: The long, thin extension multiplies the surface area in contact with soil water, so osmosis and active transport can proceed at a much higher rate.

check.stem: A seedling is transplanted with most root hairs broken off. Predict the effect and explain it.
check.modelAnswer: Water and ion uptake drops sharply, because the absorbing surface area has been lost, so the seedling wilts until new hairs grow.

lessons.title: The Route of Water Through the Plant
sourceHeadings: The route of water through the plant
lessons.opening: Once inside, water crosses the root cortex cell by cell, enters the xylem vessels at the root's core, and rides upward to the leaf mesophyll, always moving from higher to lower water potential.
keyPoints: Water travels root hair cell, then cortex cells, then xylem.
From the xylem it reaches the mesophyll cells of the leaf.
Water potential runs high in the soil, lower inside the plant.
Osmosis drives each inward step of the journey.
The xylem then carries the column upward to the leaves.

low.restatement: Soil water enters by osmosis, crosses the cortex, climbs the xylem and ends in the leaf cells.
low.analogy: A relay race: each runner (cell layer) passes the baton (water) inward until the xylem takes the long leg.
low.examPointer: Write the pathway in order and spell mesophyll correctly; sequence questions punish jumps.

medium.restatement: Each step follows the falling water potential, so the leaf's demand pulls the whole chain, from soil to mesophyll.
medium.analogy: A queue at a shop door: the empty space inside (low potential) draws people in from the crowded street (high potential).
medium.examPointer: Tie the direction to water potential explicitly; naming osmosis without the gradient loses the explanation mark.

check.stem: Which sequence gives the correct pathway of water across a root?

options.text: Root hair cell, root cortex cells, xylem
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Xylem, cortex cells, root hair cell
options.explanation: That runs backwards; uptake starts at the surface.

options.text: Root hair cell, xylem, cortex cells
options.explanation: The cortex sits between the hair and the xylem.

options.text: Cortex cells, root hair cell, xylem
options.explanation: The hair cell is the first stop, not the second.

check.stem: Water moves from the xylem into which leaf cells at the end of its journey?

options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Guard cells adjust stomata; the main destination is the mesophyll.
The epidermis is the leaf's outer skin, not the endpoint of supply.
Phloem carries sugars, not the incoming water supply.

check.stem: What decides the direction water moves at each step across the root?

options.text: The water potential gradient, from higher to lower
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: The sugar concentration of the xylem
options.explanation: Sugar is the phloem's cargo, not the water driver.
Mitochondria matter for ion pumps, not osmosis.
Colour has no role in water movement.

check.stem: Which process moves water between the cortex cells?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
That spends energy to move ions, not water.
Pull transmits tension, but the cell-to-cell step is osmosis.
Capillarity is a narrow-tube effect, not the cell route.

check.stem: Why does the soil usually supply water to the root rather than the reverse?

options.text: Soil water potential is higher than the root cell's, so osmosis points inward
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: Because the root pushes water outward at night
options.explanation: No outward push exists.
Saltier means lower potential, which would reverse the flow.

options.text: Because gravity holds water in the soil
options.explanation: Gravity acts on drainage, not on cell-level osmosis.

check.stem: Write out the pathway of water through the plant in order.
check.modelAnswer: From the root hair cell across the cortex into the xylem and finally the leaf's mesophyll.

check.stem: Define water potential in simple terms.
check.modelAnswer: It measures how freely water molecules can move in a solution.

check.stem: Explain why water keeps flowing inward even after the root hair cells are saturated.
check.modelAnswer: Because the xylem and the leaf beyond it maintain a lower water potential, so the gradient never disappears and osmosis continues inward.

check.stem: Seawater splashes onto a coastal plant's soil. Predict what happens to water uptake and justify it.
check.modelAnswer: Uptake falls or reverses, because the salt lowers the soil's water potential below that of the root cells, so osmosis no longer points inward.

glossary.definition: The diffusion of water across a membrane from higher to lower water potential.
Energy-consuming uptake of substances against their gradient.
A measure of how freely water molecules can move in a solution.
The vessels that carry water and dissolved minerals upward through a plant.
